Oral swab samples (sensitivity difference ‐33 percentage points, 95% CI ‐62 to –5; based on four evaluations, 1243 sample pairs including 257 with confirmed SARS‐CoV‐2); Oral rinse samples (sensitivity difference ‐20 percentage points, 95% CI ‐38 to –2; based on two evaluations, 238 sample pairs including 65 with confirmed SARS‐CoV‐2); Oropharyngeal samples (sensitivity difference ‐17 percentage points, 95% CI ‐29 to –5; based on seven evaluations, 2522 sample pairs including 511 with confirmed SARS‐CoV‐2); Saliva samples collected using spitting, drooling or salivating (sensitivity difference on average ‐12 percentage points, 95% CI ‐16 to ‐8, based on 56 evaluations, 27,253 sample pairs including 4636 with confirmed SARS‐CoV‐2). We did not find any evidence of a difference in the sensitivity of saliva collected using spitting, drooling or salivating (sensitivity difference ranges from ‐13 percentage points (spit) to –21 percentage points (salivate)); Nasal samples (mid‐turbinate, anterior nares and unclear collection method combined) (sensitivity difference ‐12 percentage points, 95% CI ‐17 to ‐7; based on 29 evaluations, 9291 sample pairs including 1485 with confirmed SARS‐CoV‐2). We did not find any evidence of a difference in sensitivity between nasal samples from these two collection sites with RT‐PCR. Sensitivity of nasal samples for the detection of SARS‐CoV‐2 infection with rapid antigen tests See Table and Figure . Compared to a nasopharyngeal sample, there was no evidence for a difference in sensitivity of nasal samples when used with AG‐RDTs (sensitivity difference 0 percentage points, 95% CI –0.02 to +0.02; based on eight evaluation cohorts, 3688 sample pairs including 535 with confirmed SARS‐CoV‐2). Compared to a nasopharyngeal sample, there was no evidence of a difference in sensitivity between nasal samples collected from the mid‐turbinates or from the anterior nares in rapid antigen tests. The effect of sample operator expertise on the sensitivity of sample types for the detection of SARS‐CoV‐2 infection See Figure . Two evaluations concerned the effect of operator expertise on the collection of nasopharyngeal samples. One evaluation demonstrated a reduction in sensitivity with self‐collection compared to healthcare worker (HCW) collection (sensitivity difference ‐33 percentage points, 95% CI ‐58 to ‐8; based on 50 sample pairs including 24 with confirmed SARS‐CoV‐2; Abdollahi 2020a ) and the other found no evidence of a difference in sensitivity with self‐collection compared to HCW collection (sensitivity difference 0 percentage points, 95% CI ‐16 to +16; based on 216 sample pairs including 42 with confirmed SARS‐CoV‐2; Amoo 2021 ). One evaluation assessed the effect of operator expertise on the collection of oropharyngeal samples and demonstrated no evidence of a difference in sensitivity with self‐collection compared to HCW collection (sensitivity difference ‐8 percentage points, 95% CI ‐19 to +35; based on 50 sample pairs including 25 with confirmed SARS‐CoV‐2; Abdollahi 2020b ). One evaluation cohort assessed the effect of operator expertise on the collection of saliva samples and demonstrated a reduction in sensitivity of self‐collection compared to supervised (by HCW) self‐collection (sensitivity difference ‐26 percentage points, 95% CI ‐45 to – 6; based on 44 sample pairs including 27 with confirmed SARS‐CoV‐2; Kojima 2020 ). Investigations of heterogeneity For gargle samples, oral rinse samples, oral swab samples, oropharyngeal and combined nasal/oropharyngeal samples and operator experience, we were not able to undertake any planned investigations of heterogeneity because of sparse data. For saliva studies, we investigated the effect of participant age, symptom status, and operator (HCW, self‐collection or supervised self‐collection) on sensitivity compared to a nasopharyngeal sample for all saliva collection methods combined and within subgroups of different saliva collection methods. Due to sparse data, we were only able to investigate the effect of the use of transport media and time of sample collection in relation to symptom onset for all saliva collection methods combined. For nasal samples, we were able to investigate the effect of symptom status, time of sample collection, use of transport media and operator expertise (HCW or self collection) on sensitivity compared to a nasopharyngeal sample for all nasal collection methods combined and in molecular and antigen tests combined. Saliva samples We observed a lower sensitivity in HCW collected compared to self‐collected (sensitivity difference ‐9 percentage points, 95% CI –13 to –6; based on 21,984 sample pairs including 5209 with confirmed SARS‐CoV‐2) and HCW‐collected compared to supervised self‐collected (sensitivity difference ‐14 percentage points, 95% CI –22 to –6; based on 17,251 sample pairs including 2028 with confirmed SARS‐CoV‐2) subgroups in the saliva group of studies. However, this result should be interpreted with caution as the single HCW‐collected saliva evaluation in this comparison is an outlier: Castelain 2021 (sensitivity difference ‐92 percentage points, 95% CI –103 to –82; based on 501 sample pairs including 26 with confirmed SARS‐CoV‐2). See Appendix 10 and Appendix 11 . We did not observe evidence of a difference in sensitivity for saliva samples (all collection methods combined or within collection method subgroups) compared to a nasopharyngeal sample beyond that expected by chance according to age (adult versus child) or symptom status (symptomatic versus asymptomatic). We did not observe evidence of a difference in sensitivity for saliva samples (all collection methods combined) by the time of post‐symptom onset (≤ 1 week post‐symptom onset, ≤ 2 weeks post‐symptom onset and ≤ 3 weeks post‐symptom onset) or use of transport medium (transport medium versus no transport medium) beyond that expected by chance. See Appendix 8 and Appendix 10 . Nasal samples We observed a reduction in sensitivity of nasal samples compared to a reference sample greater than would be expected by chance with increasing time post‐symptom onset: ≤ 1 week post‐symptom onset (‐2 percentage points, 95% CI –3 to –0.3; based on 6764 sample pairs including 1077 with confirmed SARS‐CoV‐2); ≤ 2 weeks post‐symptom onset (‐13 percentage points, 95% CI –23 to ‐2; based on 1808 sample pairs including 240 with confirmed SARS‐CoV‐2) and ≤ 3 weeks post‐symptom onset (‐46 percentage points, 95% CI –96 to –4; based on 569 sample pairs including 149 with confirmed SARS‐CoV‐2). See Appendix 8 and Appendix 11 . We did not observe evidence of a difference in sensitivity beyond that expected by chance for nasal samples in molecular and AG‐RDTs combined (all collection methods combined or within collection method subgroups (anterior and mid‐turbinate)) compared to a nasopharyngeal sample by symptom status (symptomatic versus asymptomatic), use of transport medium (transport medium versus no transport medium) or operator expertise (HCW verus self‐collection). Sensitivity analysis We undertook a sensitivity analysis comparing the main analyses (which included evaluations where the kit manufacturer or components of a testing kit differed across two samples in a pair) with analyses where these evaluations were removed (10 evaluations of saliva samples, five evaluations of nasal samples, two evaluations of oral swabs and one evaluation of gargle samples). We also undertook sensitivity analysis comparing the main analyses (corrections applied to studies with zero variance allowing those studies to be included in the pooled estimates) and analyses eliminating studies with a within‐study variance of the sensitivity difference equal to zero (10 evaluations of nasal samples, one evaluation of saliva samples, one evaluation of oropharyngeal samples, and one evaluation of gargle samples). Our conclusions were not changed by the results of the sensitivity analyses ( Appendix 12 ). Discussion This review summarises evidence from within‐person (direct) comparisons of the sensitivity of alternative sample sites (compared to nasopharyngeal samples) and the effect of operator expertise on the detection of SARS‐CoV‐2 in ambulatory populations. The results of this review are based on published journal articles or studies available as preprints from 1 January 2020 up until 22 February 2022. In addition, we also included evaluations that were available as independent, national reference laboratory publications or that were co‐ordinated and published by FIND, and journal articles that were listed on the Diagnostics Global Health website until 30 April 2021. Summary of main results We included data from 106 studies reporting 154 evaluations, with a total of 60,523 sample pairs (participants) and 11,045 participants with confirmed SARS‐CoV‐2. The key findings are presented in Table . We summarise nine key findings from this review below. 1. There is no evidence that the sensitivity of gargle samples or deep throat saliva samples differs from nasopharyngeal samples when used with RT‐PCR. There is no evidence of a difference in sensitivity of gargle samples or deep throat saliva samples compared to nasopharyngeal samples for the detection of SARS‐CoV‐2 with RT‐PCR. There is evidence from one study that saliva collected using a combination of swabbing and drooling has a comparable sensitivity to nasopharyngeal samples for the detection of SARS‐CoV‐2 with RT‐PCR. Considerable heterogeneity exists in the evidence base for gargle samples and deep throat saliva. 2. There is some evidence that combined oropharyngeal/nasal samples demonstrate a higher sensitivity than nasopharyngeal samples when used with RT‐PCR. There is some evidence that combined oropharyngeal/nasal samples demonstrate higher sensitivity (average +7% percentage points) compared to a nasopharyngeal sample. However, this finding is based on only four evaluations (701 sample pairs) and collection methods varied (for example, two of the four evaluation samples were collected by healthcare workers, one was self‐collected, and in one evaluation this was not stated). 3. Nasal (anterior nares and mid‐turbinate), saliva (spit, drool, salivate), oropharyngeal and oral samples demonstrate a reduction in sensitivity compared to nasopharyngeal samples when used with RT‐PCR. Nasal, saliva (spit or salivate or drool), oropharyngeal and oral samples demonstrate a reduction in sensitivity compared to nasopharyngeal samples in descending order from oral swabs (average of 33% percentage points lower), oral rinse samples (20 percentage points lower), oropharyngeal samples (17 percentage points lower), saliva (spit or drool or salivate) samples (12 percentage points lower) and nasal (anterior or mid‐turbinate) samples (12 percentage points lower). Formal, indirect statistical comparison of sensitivities by sample site were not undertaken due to substantial heterogeneity and potential confounding. Overlapping 95% confidence intervals for the summary sensitivities suggest no evidence of a difference in sensitivity between these sample types, but for oral and oropharyngeal samples, the number of evaluations is small and there is substantial imprecision in estimates. 4. There is no evidence that the sensitivity of nasal samples (anterior or mid‐turbinate) differs from nasopharyngeal samples when used with Ag‐RDTs, but the applicability of this finding to self‐testing is unclear. Evidence for the accuracy of different sample types used with rapid antigen tests was limited in our review. In eight evaluations, there was no evidence of a difference in sensitivity of nasal samples compared to nasopharyngeal samples when used with rapid antigen tests. Only three of five evaluations of Ag‐RDTs documented collection methods and, in these three evaluations, the sample was interpreted by a healthcare professional or self‐collected and interpreted whilst supervised by a healthcare professional. It is therefore unclear the extent to which estimates of sample sensitivity for use with rapid antigen tests represent self‐sampling, self‐testing or healthcare worker testing. 5. There is no evidence that the sensitivity of saliva samples changes with increasing time post‐symptom onset. We did not find any evidence that the sensitivity of saliva samples differed with time post‐symptom onset, but conclusions are limited by the relatively small number of studies ≥ 3 weeks post‐symptom onset. In nasal samples, sensitivity decreased with time, from minus two percentage points at one week post‐symptom onset to ‐46 percentage points at three weeks post‐symptom onset compared to nasopharyngeal samples. The finding of a decline in sensitivity over time in nasal samples is in line with existing evidence ( Mallett 2020 ; Weiss 2020 ; Wolfel 2020 ). The lack of a decline in the sensitivity of saliva samples (all collection methods combined) over time may be a reflection of the presence of secretions from the lower respiratory tract in deep throat saliva. Viral load has been shown to decrease more slowly in the lower respiratory tract compared to the upper respiratory tract ( Mallett 2020 ; Weiss 2020 ). 6. Poor reporting hampers quality assessment. Only 3% of included evaluations were at low risk of bias overall. However, poor reporting precluded reliable quality assessment. Most evaluations were judged as having unclear risk of bias (59% in the flow and timing domain, 74% in the participant domain and 77% in the index test domain). Where risk of bias assessment was possible, methodological concerns included enrichment of cohorts with confirmed SARS‐CoV‐2‐positive participants, inappropriate exclusions (for example, because of an inability to collect sufficient sample volume), lack of blinding between samples being compared, non‐random ordering of samples being compared, and incomplete recording and/or analysis of excluded, lost or invalid samples. Similarly, poor reporting precluded assessment of applicability in the participant (77%) and index test (38%) domains. In particular, only 38% of evaluation cohorts reported time of testing with reference to symptom onset in symptomatic participants, which may confound results, particularly in index groups or subgroups containing few evaluations. The most likely impact of confounding in this review will be to undermine our assessment of the relative sensitivity of different collection methods and of different anatomical sampling sites relative to one another. 7. Poor reporting and sparse data limited investigations of heterogeneity. Age, symptom status and use of transport media do not appear to affect the sensitivity of saliva and nasal samples. We were limited by sparse data and were only able to perform some of our planned investigations of heterogeneity in saliva and nasal samples. We did not find any difference in sensitivity according to age or symptom status for any sample type, although the number of evaluations in children (saliva 6/90, 6.4%) and nasal (1/37, 2.7%), respectively, and in asymptomatic participants (saliva 6/90, 6.7%) and nasal (1/37, 2.7%), respectively, was relatively small. We did not find any evidence that the use of transport media affected the sensitivity of saliva samples or nasal samples. For nasal samples, the number of evaluations without transport media was small (7/37, 18.8%) and so the implications of this finding are unclear. However, for saliva samples, approximately half the total number of evaluations were performed without transport media (42/90, 46.7%), which increases our certainty in this finding. The effect of operator expertise on the sensitivity of samples is unclear. We only identified four evaluations that investigated the effect of operator expertise on the sensitivity of samples, and our ability to investigate operator expertise as a source of heterogeneity in this review was limited by lack of reporting and sparse data. Findings are conflicting, and where we had evidence, we found no consistent effect of operator expertise on the sensitivity of nasopharyngeal, oropharyngeal, nasal or saliva samples when used with RT‐PCR. Data were too sparse to investigate the effect of operator experience on the sensitivity of nasal samples in Ag‐RDTs. 8. Most of the evidence about alternatives to nasopharyngeal swabs has been conducted with RT‐PCR and concerns self‐sampling. Most (146, 95%) evaluations were conducted with molecular tests and, of these, 140 (91%) were conducted with RT‐PCR. Only eight evaluations using nasal samples were conducted with Ag‐RDTs. Many of the index samples used for molecular tests were self‐collected (57%) or self‐collected whilst supervised by a healthcare professional (23%). Most of the evaluations of samples for use with RT‐PCR in this review, therefore, relate to self‐sampling. 9. Evidence about the sensitivity of different sample types is lacking in children and in asymptomatic populations. Median SARS‐CoV‐2 prevalence across evaluation cohorts was 23%. Twenty‐eight of 154 evaluations were conducted in mixed populations but only seven (5%) evaluations were conducted on children. This is particularly important given that most of the samples in this review were self‐collected. The accuracy of samples reported in this review may not be replicable in children. Many evaluations were conducted in dedicated COVID‐19 testing clinics or in ambulatory hospital settings (55%). Testing in the context of targeted screening or contact tracing accounted for only 4% of evaluations. This is reflected by the fact that 46% of evaluations were conducted in mixed symptomatic and asymptomatic populations, whilst only seven (5%) were conducted in asymptomatic populations. We were not able to demonstrate any effect of symptom status on the sensitivity of different sample types in this review, which may point to our findings being applicable in symptomatic and asymptomatic populations. Alternatively, the lack of an effect of symptom status in this body of evidence may be an artefact as a result of the relatively low number of asymptomatic evaluation cohorts contributing to this subgroup analysis. Strengths and weaknesses of the review To our knowledge, this is the most up‐to‐date and comprehensive summary of the evidence for the sensitivity of different sample sites and collection processes for the detection of SARS‐CoV‐2, based on within‐person (direct) comparisons. Our review results have increased certainty in, and are broadly consistent with, existing systematic reviews with respect to nasal/oropharyngeal ( Lee 2021 ), deep throat saliva ( Butler‐Laporte 2021 ) and gargle ( Tsang 2022 ) achieving the highest sensitivities compared to nasopharyngeal samples. Oropharyngeal, undifferentiated saliva and undifferentiated nasal sample sensitivities were between 12 and 18 percentage points lower than nasopharyngeal samples when used with RT‐PCR ( Atieh 2021 ; Bastos 2021 ; Butler‐Laporte 2021 ; Kivela 2021 ; Lee 2021 ). In addition, this review has been able to examine the sensitivity of alternative nasal (anterior nares and mid‐turbinate) samples and saliva (salivate, swab and drool) collection techniques, the sensitivity of oral samples and the effect of operator expertise on sensitivity. Due to a larger body of evidence, compared to previous reviews, we have been able to investigate the effect of symptom status, age, use of transport media and time post‐symptom onset on the sensitivity of nasal and saliva sample types. This review also presents within‐person evidence for the sensitivity difference of nasal compared to nasopharyngeal samples for use with Ag‐RDTs. Our review used a broad search, screening all articles concerning COVID‐19 or SARS‐CoV‐2. We undertook all screening and eligibility assessments, QUADAS‐2 ( Whiting 2011 ) and QUADAS‐C ( Yang 2021 ) assessments, and data extraction of study findings independently and in duplicate. Although it is possible that the use of artificial intelligence text analysis to identify studies most relevant to diagnostic questions may have led to some eligible studies being missed, we believe that the multi‐stranded search strategy used will have identified most, if not all, relevant literature. We have reasonable confidence in the completeness and accuracy of the findings up until the search date. The robustness of our findings depends on the quality of the sample pair comparisons. To this end, we restricted inclusion to within‐person comparison of sample pairs in participants suspected of having SARS‐CoV‐2 infection at the time of testing, with both sample types included in the comparison. We excluded studies where participants were exclusively preselected for inclusion based on being known as SARS‐CoV‐2‐positive in the reference sample. We further restricted studies to those where the samples being compared were collected within the same clinical encounter, excluding studies where time between collection of different sample types was reported as being longer than 24 hours. We undertook quality assessment of the sample pair comparison using items from the QUADAS‐C checklist for comparative diagnostic test accuracy studies ( Yang 2021 ), interrogating included studies for comparability of the sampling process (for example, operator skill, unless this was the sampling variable being compared), extraction process, type of SARS‐CoV‐2 test, gene targets, and disease positivity threshold. We also assessed included studies for bias that may be introduced by the order in which samples were taken (for example, comparison of oropharyngeal samples with nasopharyngeal/oropharyngeal samples and nasal samples with nasopharyngeal samples). The analytical approach to this review precludes estimation of specificity. We consider that the occurrence of false positives would be negligible for molecular and antigen‐based tests ( Dinnes 2022 ) and similar between sample sites. We assume that the impact of false negatives from the testing technology (molecular or antigen in this review) on the validity of estimates of differences in sensitivity will be minimised, provided the testing method is the same for each sample in a pair and assuming that false negatives from different sample types are not independent. The validity of our estimates of the comparative sensitivity of sample pairs, therefore, depends on the assumption that differences in false negatives arise only as a result of differences in the sample type or process being investigated, rather than other elements of the sampling and testing process. In 141/154 (92%) sample pair comparisons, the same extraction and testing kits were used for each sample in a pair. For 13 sample pair comparisons (7/90 saliva samples, 3/37 nasal samples, 2/6 oral samples and 1/7 oropharyngeal samples), extraction and/or testing were undertaken using the same method but different testing kits for each sample in a pair. A sensitivity analysis in affected index tests did not demonstrate an effect of differences in the testing process on estimates of sensitivity. The main limitations of this review arise as a result of limitations in the evidence base. Poor reporting of the sampling process itself, such as the order in which samples were collected and blinding of interpretation between index and reference samples in 77% of included evaluations, undermined a comprehensive assessment of the validity of sample comparisons. Except for saliva and nasal samples, the number of studies contributing to accuracy estimates was small, reducing our confidence in the reliability of our findings and precluding planned investigations of heterogeneity in oropharyngeal, combined nasal/oropharyngeal, gargle and oral samples. The number of evaluations in Ag‐RDTs was small and was restricted to evaluations of nasal samples. Poor reporting hampered a comprehensive assessment of methodological quality and applicability and further undermined investigations of heterogeneity. In 62% of evaluations, the time of sampling in relation to symptom onset was not stated. Most of the included studies did not report the occurrence or management of indeterminate results, which precluded sensitivity analysis investigating the effect of these on estimates of accuracy or commenting on the effect of this on the clinical utility of different sample types. Our approach to analysis of studies where indeterminate results were reported was to classify these as 'positive' for estimation of sensitivity. This approach was taken because indeterminate results are more aligned to a positive rather than a negative test result in terms of clinical action and impact on the person tested, and because excludng indeterminate results would have resulted in overestimation of sensitivity. Although our inclusion criteria and (where reported) most (67%) evaluations were undertaken within one week of symptom onset, we cannot rule out the effect of confounding by time since symptom onset on our comparison of the relative accuracy of different index sample types compared to a nasopharyngeal sample. Despite the search date of this review (22 February 2022), we consider it unlikely that research conducted since the completion of searches would alter the conclusions. Applicability of findings to the review question Most (81%) studies recruited participants prospectively on the basis of a suspicion of SARS‐CoV‐2 infection. Participants were symptomatic (33%) or mixed symptomatic and asymptomatic (46%) and the median prevalence was 23% (IQR 13% to 40%). Most (69%) studies were conducted in dedicated COVID‐19 testing centres and community or outpatient settings. Less than 4% of included evaluations were conducted in the context of targeted screening (for example, in school or hospital settings) or as part of contact tracing. Our ability to explore whether the accuracy of samples varied according to symptom status was limited, but did not appear to have an effect on the sensitivity of saliva sample evaluations. The applicability of these findings to asymptomatic, screening populations is unclear. We aimed to include studies recruiting individuals early in the course of infection. Only one‐third of evaluation cohorts (58/154) reported time of testing with reference to symptom onset in symptomatic participants. However, in most of these, 58 evaluation cohorts testing, this was undertaken within one week of symptom onset (67%) and in a minority (10%), up to three weeks post‐symptom onset. Our ability to quantify any difference in sensitivity over time post‐symptom onset with different sample types was therefore limited. Existing evidence demonstrates superior test performance with upper respiratory tract samples for symptomatic participants in the first 7 to 10 days post‐symptom onset ( Dinnes 2022 ; Mallett 2020 ; Weiss 2020 ; Wolfel 2020 ), probably corresponding with higher viral loads ( Cevik 2021 ). We consider that estimates of sensitivity for the majority of (upper respiratory) sample types in this review are likely to be the most optimistic of those possible. Virus is more likely to be detected by lower respiratory tract samples and nonrespiratory tract samples after this time. The finding in this review, that the sensitivity of saliva samples (as a nonrespiratory tract sample) does not appear to decline over time, is compatible with existing research concerned with lower respiratory tract samples ( Mallett 2020 ; Weiss 2020 ). In the evaluations conducted with RT‐PCR, only seven were conducted on children and most (80%) index samples were self‐collected. In the rapid antigen evaluations, none were conducted on children and in the three where this was reported, only one was self‐collected whilst being supervised by a healthcare worker (HCW). Our findings for evaluations conducted with RT‐PCR are therefore applicable to self‐collected samples by adults. For evaluations conducted with rapid antigen tests, it is unclear the extent to which estimates represent healthcare worker testing, self‐sampling or self‐testing in adults. Authors' conclusions Implications for practice This review summarises evidence of the sensitivity of alternative anatomical sample collection sites and collection methods to healthcare worker‐collected nasopharyngeal samples for the detection of SARS‐CoV‐2. Most of the evidence is from symptomatic adults presenting to dedicated COVID‐19 testing centres. Evidence about the sensitivity of sample types in asymptomatic populations and in children is lacking. The implications of this on the applicability of our findings are unclear due to limitations in our investigations of heterogeneity. For confirmatory testing with NAATs for detection of SARS‐CoV‐2, the WHO, CDC and ECDC recommend an upper respiratory tract (URT) sample in VTM, with the WHO specifying a combined nasopharyngeal/oropharyngeal specimen ( WHO 2020b ). CDC recommend saliva as an alternative to URT samples for confirmatory testing with NAATs in symptomatic individuals only when nasopharyngeal samples cannot be collected ( Centres for Disease Control 2021 ), and ECDC recommends saliva only with assays detecting SARS‐CoV‐2 RNA ( ECDC 2021 ). There is evidence in this review to suggest that self‐collected, combined nasal/oropharyngeal, self‐collected gargle samples and self‐collected deep throat saliva have comparable sensitivity to healthcare worker‐collected nasopharyngeal samples when used with RT‐PCR. Self‐collected samples have the potential to reduce exposure of healthcare staff to infection and negate the need for Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) with associated resource savings. This review also provides evidence that direct sampling (without the use of transport media) of nasal samples and saliva samples does not result in a decrease in sensitivity. The use of deep throat saliva with RT‐PCR, therefore, has, in addition, the potential to save resources and reduce complexity when confirmatory testing is needed at scale. Further, there is evidence from this review that the sensitivity of saliva samples does not appear to decline with increasing time post‐symptom onset. This is in contrast to a decline in sensitivity with increasing time post‐symptom onset observed with nasal samples in this review, which mirrors the decline in sensitivity with increasing time post‐symptom onset observed with URT in other reviews ( Mallett 2020 ; Weiss 2020 ; Wolfel 2020 ). This may be an important consideration for choice of sample type in individuals presenting for testing later in the course of the disease. Self‐collected saliva (spit, salivate and drool), nasal (mid‐turbinate and anterior nares), oropharyngeal and oral swabs have a lower sensitivity of similar magnitude compared to nasopharyngeal samples when used with RT‐PCR. However, the volume of evidence for oropharyngeal and oral samples is relatively small and imprecise. Despite the advantages associated with self‐collected compared to healthcare‐collected samples, and for saliva and nasal samples, the advantages offered by direct sampling, the reduction in sensitivity compared to healthcare worker‐collected nasopharyngeal swabs with these sample types may not be acceptable in testing settings where the purpose of testing is confirmation of SARS‐CoV‐2 infection. For rapid antigen tests, WHO, CDC and ECDC recommend URT samples. A limited body of homogenous evidence in this review suggests that nasal samples have comparable accuracy to nasopharyngeal samples when used with rapid antigen tests. Further, we found no evidence for a difference in sensitivity of nasal mid‐turbinate and nasal anterior nares samples. This is an important finding for rapid tests as the acceptability of sample collection is likely to be an even more important factor affecting testing uptake in asymptomatic individuals in the community. However, it is unclear in this review the extent to which sensitivity estimates generated from nasal samples used with rapid antigen tests were based on self‐collection. These estimates may therefore not be replicable outside of healthcare settings. We did not find any direct, within‐person comparisons of other sample types used with rapid antigen tests. Estimates of the sensitivity of nasal samples used with rapid antigen tests from another review (not restricted to within sample comparisons) in this series suggested a similar sensitivity compared to nasopharyngeal samples ( Dinnes 2022 ). In the same review, saliva samples used with rapid antigen tests had a lower sensitivity compared to nasopharyngeal samples (‐36.8 percentage points, 95% CI ‐43.5 to ‐30.1). Where samples have comparable sensitivity and resource implications, the acceptability of the sampling process is an important consideration. Nasal samples have been shown to cause less discomfort than oropharyngeal swabs ( Frazee 2018 ), and research has shown a preference for saliva over nasal samples ( McLaughlin 2022 ). Importantly, in this review, we were not able to demonstrate a difference in sensitivity between nasal mid‐turbinate and nasal anterior nares samples, which may have implications for the acceptability of nasal samples. However, acceptability will differ in different population groups. For example, some individuals may struggle to generate a saliva sample ( Blackmore 2020 ). A recent study evaluated the ease of self‐collection of direct saliva samples for individuals presenting for SARS‐CoV‐2 testing, and although 90% of participants perceived saliva collection as simple, one‐third of participants had difficulty collecting a sufficient saliva sample volume and 26% of saliva samples required additional processing to reduce viscosity with adverse consequences for laboratory workflow ( Plantamura 2021 ). In this review, indeterminate or invalid results were reported by 40% of saliva evaluation cohorts, 33% of gargle evaluation cohorts and 24% of nasal evaluation cohorts. For saliva, invalid samples were most often a result of inadequate sample volume or because of hyper‐viscosity of samples. Implications for research Combined nasal/oropharyngeal, gargle samples and deep throat saliva show promise as superior or comparable sample types for use with RT‐PCR. More research is needed to increase certainty that these alternative samples can achieve the sensitivity required in settings where confirmation of SARS‐CoV‐2 infection (with RT‐PCR) is the goal of testing. There is a considerable body of research concerned with the sensitivity of saliva and nasal samples used with RT‐PCR in symptomatic and mixed symptom status populations. Evidence for the accuracy of other sample types for use with RT‐PCR is lacking. Further research is needed to determine whether oral and oropharyngeal samples have comparable sensitivity to samples where estimates of sensitivity are based on a larger volume of evidence: nasal (anterior and mid‐turbinate) and saliva (drool, salivate and spit) samples. The findings of this review suggest that, in contrast to upper respiratory tract samples, the sensitivity of saliva samples may not decrease as rapidly with increasing time post‐symptom onset. Viral load is likely to be higher in symptomatic populations, and it has been demonstrated that virus is cleared more rapidly from samples from children ( Weiss 2020 ). Children and asymptomatic individuals were under‐represented in this review. More research is needed to determine whether this finding in predominantly adult, symptomatic individuals is replicable in child and asymptomatic populations within different saliva collection methods and in testing technologies other than RT‐PCR. Evidence about the sensitivity of different sample types in asymptomatic populations and in children is lacking. This may be a reflection of the lack of evidence for the effect of different sample types and operator experience for the detection of SARS‐CoV‐2 with rapid antigen tests. Although there is evidence from this review that nasal (anterior or mid‐turbinate) samples have comparable sensitivity to nasopharyngeal samples with rapid antigen tests, poor reporting means it is unclear the extent to which this represents healthcare‐worker testing, self‐sampling or self‐testing. The lack of evaluations of different samples and factors that might affect the accuracy of sample collection and interpretation in testing technologies other than RT‐PCR is an important omission given the important role of rapid antigen self‐testing in pandemic and epidemic settings. Poor reporting precluded adequate quality assessment and assessment of applicability for evidence in this review; just over half (62%) of samples provided sufficient information to allow replication of sample collection. Similarly, only 31% of evaluation cohorts (48/154) reported invalid and uninterpretable results. Future within‐person evaluations should recruit a consecutive sample of participants and provide information about age, time of testing in relation to symptom onset, and exposure. Sampling (and interpretation of rapid antigen tests) procedure should be detailed, including any instruction or training of sample collectors, extraction and testing kits used, and thresholds should be documented. To minimise bias in sample comparisons, authors should carefully consider the potential for contamination of different sample types when deciding on sample order, or randomise the order of sample collection. Interpretation of test results for each sample type should be conducted blind to other sample results. Eligibility and exclusion decisions (including test failures) throughout the whole diagnostic pathway should conform to the updated Standards for Reporting of Diagnostic Accuracy (STARD) guidelines ( Bossuyt 2015 ). Search classification model Search classification model, used from 25 May 2020 We needed a more efficient approach to keep up with the rapidly increasing volume of COVID‐19 literature. A classification model for COVID‐19 diagnostic studies was built with the model‐building function within Eppi Reviewer, which uses the standard SGDClassifier in Scikit‐learn on word trigrams. As outputs, new documents receive a percentage (from the predict_proba function), where scores close to 100 indicate a high probability of belonging to the class ‘relevant document’ and scores close to 0 indicate a low probability of belonging to the class ‘relevant document’. We used three iterations of manual screening (title and abstract screening, followed by full‐text review) to build and test classifiers. The final included studies were used as relevant documents, while the remainder of the COVID‐19 studies were used as irrelevant documents. The classifier was trained on the first round of selected articles, and tested and retrained on the second round of selected articles. Testing on the second round of selected articles revealed poor positive predictive value but 100% sensitivity at a cut‐off of 10. The poor positive predictive value is mainly due to the broad scope of our topic (all diagnostic studies in COVID‐19), poor reporting in abstracts, and a small set of included documents. The model was retrained using the articles selected from the second and third rounds of screening, which added a considerable number of additional documents. This led to a large increase in positive predictive value, at the cost of a lower sensitivity, which led us to reduce the cut‐off to 5. The largest proportion of documents had a score between 0 and 5. This set did not contain any of the relevant documents. This version of the classifier with a cut‐off 5 was used in subsequent rounds and accounted for approximately 80% of the screening burden. Appendix 5. documents.title: Phase-resolved MRI for measurement of pulmonary perfusion and ventilation defects in comparison with dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI and <sup>129</sup>Xe MRI.
documents.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: This meta-analysis aims to evaluate the agreement and correlation between phase-resolved functional lung MRI (PREFUL MRI) and dynamic contrast-enhanced (DCE) MRI in evaluating perfusion defect percentage (QDP), as well as the agreement between PREFUL MRI and 129Xe MRI in assessing ventilation defect percentage (VDP).
METHOD: A systematic search was conducted in the Medline, Embase and Cochrane Library databases to identify relevant studies comparing QDP and VDP measured by DCE MRI and 129Xe MRI compared with PREFUL MRI. Meta-analytical techniques were applied to calculate the pooled weighted bias, limits of agreement (LOA) and correlation coefficient. The publication bias was assessed using Egger's regression test, while heterogeneity was assessed using Cochran's Q test and Higgins I2 statistic.
RESULTS: A total of 399 subjects from 10 studies were enrolled. The mean difference and LOA were -2.31% (-8.01% to 3.40%) for QDP and 0.34% (-4.94% to 5.62%) for VDP. The pooled correlations (95% CI) were 0.65 (0.55 to 0.73) for QDP and 0.72 (0.61 to 0.80) for VDP. Furthermore, both QDP and VDP showed a negative correlation with forced expiratory volume in 1 s (FEV1). The pooled correlation between QDP and FEV1 was -0.51 (-0.74 to -0.18), as well as between VDP and FEV1 was -0.60 (-0.73 to -0.44).
CONCLUSIONS: PREFUL MRI is a promising imaging for the assessment of lung function, as it demonstrates satisfactory deviations and LOA when compared with DEC MRI and 129Xe MRI.
PROSPERO REGISTRATION NUMBER: CRD42023430847.

WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ON THIS TOPIC WHAT THIS STUDY ADDS The PREFUL MRI demonstrates high accuracy and good consistency in quantifying pulmonary perfusion defects and ventilation defects, showing a strong correlation with existing clinically reliable methods. It holds promise as a long-term pulmonary function assessment method for patients with chronic lung diseases. HOW THIS STUDY MIGHT AFFECT RESEARCH, PRACTICE OR POLICY The application of PREFUL MRI in pulmonary diseases provides patients with a convenient and non-invasive method for lung functional imaging, enabling early diagnosis and treatment assessment of pulmonary conditions. Introduction Pulmonary diseases are closely linked to structural changes in the lungs, making morphological evaluation crucial for patient assessment. However, during the early stages, the disease process predominantly affects pulmonary function while exhibiting limited modifications in pulmonary morphology. 1 Spirometry is widely used to assess the ventilatory function, which provides a global assessment of lung function but exhibits limited sensitivity to early functional changes. 2 Lung functional imaging provides the capability to identify regional lung lesions, enabling enhanced evaluation of lung diseases prior to the manifestation of global functional and morphological alterations. 3 Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a heterogeneous disease, and patients with different phenotypes respond differently to therapeutic drugs. Functional lung imaging contributes to the analysis of disease phenotypes in patients with COPD, providing potential benefits for drug screening and optimising treatment. 4 The development of hyperpolarised noble gas MRI imaging as a viable technique for ventilation imaging has been underway. 5 6 Such using 129 Xe ventilation MRI, it is possible to calculate the ventilation defect percentage (VDP), which represents the proportion of the lung that is non-ventilated. 7 VDP has been proven to be a reliable and sensitive clinical outcome measure for assessing longitudinal lung disease changes in patients with cystic fibrosis (CF). 8 9 Nevertheless, the clinical adoption of this technique has been limited due to its reliance on specialised polariser equipment. Dynamic contrast-enhanced (DCE) MRI is commonly used to assess pulmonary perfusion and volume, enabling quantification of the perfusion defect percentage (QDP). 10 11 DCE MRI has demonstrated its capability to offer quantitative assessments and has been successfully employed in the evaluation of various diseases, including COPD, CF and chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH). 11 , 13 Furthermore, DCE MRI has been demonstrated to discriminate idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) and serve as a biomarker for the progression of IPF disease. 14 However, DCE MRI requires breath holding and injection of a gadolinium-containing contrast agent, and the long-term effects of gadolinium deposition in the brain are unknown. 15 Fourier decomposition (FD) MRI has been shown to provide quantitative assessment of pulmonary ventilation under free breathing and without the need for contrast media. 16 Recently, a postprocessing technique, phase-resolved functional lung (PREFUL) imaging, has been introduced to enhance temporal resolution and enable the quantitative evaluation of regional perfusion and ventilation dynamics. 17 Distinguishing from FD MRI, PREFUL is different in several aspects: first, PREFUL performs perfusion/ventilation filtering with broad high-pass/low-pass filtering, while FD employs peak integration; second, PREFUL computes ventilation amplitudes in the time domain, contrasting with FD’s frequency domain computation; additionally, PREFUL sorts images based on their phase to reconstruct cardiac/ventilation cycles with enhanced temporal resolution. 17 18 Extensive investigations have demonstrated consistent measurement outcomes between PREFUL MRI and DCE MRI in detecting regional pulmonary QDP across various lung diseases. 11 19 20 Similarly, there is concordance between PREFUL MRI and 129 Xe MRI in assessing regional VDP. 21 Additionally, prior studies have revealed a significant correlation between PREFUL MRI and spirometry-derived forced expiratory volume in 1 s (FEV 1 ). 13 20 21 Although multiple studies have evaluated the accuracy of PREFUL MRI in assessing lung function, each study included only a small number of patients, necessitating caution in making generalisations and broader interpretations. Therefore, the primary objective of this meta-analysis was to systematically assess the agreement and correlation of PREFUL MRI with DCE MRI and 129 Xe MRI of lung function parameters. Additionally, we also assessed the correlation of QDP and VDP derived from PREFUL MRI with the FEV 1 derived from spirometry. Methods This study followed the guidelines of the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses. 22 This study was registered in PROSPERO with ID number CRD42023430847. Search strategy A systematic search was conducted in Medline, Embase and Cochrane Library databases to identify relevant articles that compared QDP and VDP as measured by PREFUL MRI, DCE MRI and 129 Xe MRI. The search was limited to articles published until 27 October 2023. Two authors independently carried out the search process, and any discrepancies were resolved through mutual agreement and consensus. An exhaustive search of the literature was conducted using a combination of keywords, either in MeSH or ‘free text’ terms: ‘phase-resolved functional lung magnetic resonance imaging’ OR ‘PREFUL MRI’ OR ‘free‐breathing proton magnetic resonance imaging’ OR ‘free-breathing 1 H magnetic resonance imaging’ OR ‘dynamic contrast‐enhanced magnetic resonance imaging’ OR ‘DCE MRI’ OR ‘ 129 Xe magnetic resonance imaging’ OR ‘ 129 Xe MRI’ AND ‘perfusion defect percentage’ OR ‘QDP’ OR ‘ventilation defect percentage’ OR ‘VDP’ OR ‘forced expiratory volume in the first second’ OR ‘FEV 1 ’. For a full comprehensive search strategy, see online supplemental file 1 . Study selection The inclusion criteria for study selection were determined according to the following criteria: (1) studies provided detailed information on the MRI scan parameters, including the scan sequence, image processing software and processing method; (2) studies included comprehensive descriptions of the study methodology and demographic data of the participants; (3) Bland-Altman analysis was employed to assess the consistency between the different MRI imaging methods; (4) Spearman or Pearson coefficient was used to evaluate the correlation between the two modalities; (5) studies included the provision of QDP or VDP parameters for PREFUL MRI, QDP parameter for DCE MRI, VDP parameter for 129 Xe MRI and FEV 1 measurement obtained through spirometry. Exclusion criteria for the meta-analysis involved the exclusion of animal studies and papers written in languages other than English. Additionally, abstracts, letters, editorials and meta-analyses were excluded due to lacking Bland-Altman or Pearson analysis data. The meta-analysis included both prospective and retrospective studies, as long as they met the inclusion criteria. The study population was not restricted, encompassing both adults and children, as well as patients and healthy volunteers, as long as they fulfilled the inclusion criteria. Data extraction The following data were extracted by two investigators: (1) information related to the articles, such as authors, publication journal, the total number of subjects and demographic and disease characteristics of participants; (2) MRI acquisition sequences and protocols; (3) postprocessing analysis methods employed for the calculation of QDP and VDP, along with the dedicated software used for postprocessing; (4) outcomes derived from the Bland-Altman analysis, including the mean difference (MD) and limits of agreement (LOA) for QDP between PREFUL MRI and DCE MRI, as well as VDP between PREFUL MRI and 129 Xe MRI; (5) Spearman or Pearson correlation coefficient (r) values of QDP and VDP between the two imaging methods, and the correlation between FEV 1 and QDP and VDP. The Spearman coefficients reported in the publications were transformed into Pearson coefficients. 23 24 Furthermore, Fisher’s r-to-z transformation was applied to obtain the Pearson coefficient values. 25 Quality assessment The assessment of bias risk in each included study was conducted using the modified Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies-2 (QUADAS-2) tool via Review Manager V.5.3. 26 This tool is frequently employed for the assessment of the quality of diagnostic studies. Statistical analysis The MD, LOA and r values from each study were weighted based on the sample size using a random-effects model. A modified forest plot was created to visualise the meta-analysis results for bias and LOA of each parameter. Pooled correlation coefficients for each parameter were displayed in a forest plot. Heterogeneity among the included studies was assessed using the Cochrane Q test and expressed as I 2 . Moderate to severe heterogeneity was considered present if the p value was less than 0.05 for the Q test or if I 2 exceeded 50%. Publication biases were evaluated using Egger’s test and represented through funnel plots. All statistical analyses were conducted using R (V.4.2.2, R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria) with the meta package and Review Manager (V.5.3, The Cochrane Collaboration 2021, The Nordic Cochrane Centre, Copenhagen, Denmark). Results Study selection Following the systematic search, a total of 105 citations from Medline, 456 from Embase and 6 from Cochrane were identified. After removing duplicates, 508 potentially eligible articles remained. Through the screening of titles and abstracts, 413 studies were excluded for irrelevant topics, animal models, case reports, reviews or guidelines. A total of 95 articles underwent full-text review. After a thorough evaluation based on the inclusion criteria, an additional 85 publications were excluded for reasons such as being non-English, focusing on other parameters, having unextractable data or potentially containing duplicate patient data. Finally, 10 studies met the inclusion criteria and were included in the meta-analysis. The flow chart illustrating the process of literature search and study selection can be found in figure 1 . 1319 , 21 27 Figure 1 Flow chart depicting the study review process in accordance with the guidelines provided by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA). Study characteristics The meta-analysis comprised a total of 10 studies, including 399 participants: 101 with CF, 150 with COPD, 66 with CTEPH and 82 healthy volunteers. QDP was analysed in 4 studies, VDP in 4 studies and FEV 1 in 8 studies. Table 1 presents a summary of the characteristics of the enrolled studies and details regarding MRI image acquisition. Among the studies, a 1.5-tesla (T) system was used in all except for Munidasa et al 29 and Couch et al , 28 which used a 3 T system. The most commonly used acquisition sequence for PREFUL MRI was the spoiled gradient echo (SPGR), and all DCE MRI acquisitions employed the time-resolved angiography with stochastic trajectories sequence. Five studies reported enrolling consecutive patients, while in five studies, the method of patient enrolment was not clearly explained. The risk of bias in the ‘index test’ or ‘reference standard’ domains was assessed as ‘unclear’ in six studies due to the absence of information regarding whether the MRI results were interpreted with knowledge of each other. The majority of studies (89%) demonstrated a low risk of bias in the ‘flow’ and ‘timing’ domains. Applicability concerns across all domains were rated as ‘low’. Figure 2 Quality assessment of included studies by modified Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies-2 (QUADAS-2) tool. Each bar shows the percentage of studies with high (red), unclear (yellow) and low (green) risks of bias and applicability of concerns. Publication bias Figure 3 displays the funnel plots for each parameter. The funnel plots for all parameters exhibited a relatively symmetric shape, suggesting no significant publication bias (p>0.05), except for the agreement of QDP, which showed remarkable publication bias (p=0.017). Figure 3 Funnel plots were employed to identify potential publication bias. Each circle in the plots represents a study included in the analysis. Agreement and correlation for measurements of QDP Among the included studies, three reported the MD and LOA for QDP as assessed by Bland-Altman analysis between PREFUL MRI and DCE MRI. One of these studies analysed three different groups of patient results. 13 The MD of QDP was −2.31%, with a pooled LOA ranging from −8.01% to 3.40% ( figure 4A ). Significant heterogeneity was observed (I 2 =82%, p<0.01). In addition, the pooled correlation coefficient for QDP was 0.65 (95% CI 0.55 to 0.73), with low heterogeneity (I 2 =0%, p=0.44). Agreement and correlation for measurements of VDP Four studies investigated the correlation of VDP between PREFUL MRI and 129 Xe MRI. However, only three studies reported the agreement for VDP assessment using Bland-Altman analysis. The overall MD for VDP was 0.34%, and the pooled LOA ranged from −4.94% to 5.62%. Notably, there was significant heterogeneity observed in the finding (I 2 =89%, p<0.01). Furthermore, the pooled correlation coefficient for VDP was 0.72 (95% CI 0.61 to 0.80), with mild heterogeneity (I 2 =40%, p=0.14). Figures4B 5B provide forest plots of these results. Correlation between PREFUL MRI and FEV 1 of spirometry The meta-analysis including four studies revealed a pooled correlation coefficient of −0.51 (95% CI −0.74 to −0.18) between QDP and FEV 1 . The analysis also indicated significant heterogeneity among the studies (I 2 =83%, p<0.01). Moreover, in seven studies, the pooled correlation coefficient between VDP and FEV 1 was −0.60 (95% CI −0.73 to −0.44), with a significant heterogeneity (I 2 =70%, p<0.01). All the results are shown in figure 5C,D . Discussion To the best of our understanding, this meta-analysis is the first systematic investigation of pulmonary function assessment using PREFUL MRI in comparison to DCE MRI and 129 Xe MRI. The analysis includes a total of 10 studies involving 399 subjects. The findings indicate that the evaluation of QDP on PREFUL MRI demonstrates good agreement (MD, −2.31%; LOA, −8.01% to 3.40%) and moderate correlations (r=0.65; 95% CI 0.55 to 0.73) with DCE MRI, although notable heterogeneities are observed among the studies. Furthermore, the results reveal that VDP on PREFUL MRI exhibits favourable agreement (MD, 0.34%; LOA, −4.94% to 5.62%) and strong correlations (r=0.72; 95% CI 0.61 to 0.80) with 129 Xe MRI. These findings suggest that free-breathing, non-contrast agents PREFUL MRI may allow for pulmonary perfusion and ventilation assessment comparable to DCE MRI and 129 Xe MRI. DCE MRI is a well-established and widely used technique for assessing lung perfusion. Recent studies have demonstrated that DCE MRI achieves comparable diagnostic accuracy when compared with planar scintigraphy and ventilation/perfusion scans. 33 Furthermore, investigations have shown significant correlations and spatial agreement between perfusion-weighted PREFUL MRI and DCE MRI measurements. 34 However, it is worth noting that previous research findings have been based on limited sample sizes. In our meta-analysis, we provide robust evidence supporting the clinical practice of PREFUL MRI. Notably, when considering the study by Behrendt et al , 13 we observed a larger pooled MD and the LOA. This can be attributed to incomplete breath holding during DCE data acquisition, resulting in residual movement and artificially elevated perfusion values near the diaphragm. The majority of studies used an SPGR sequence to acquire PREFUL algorithm images at 1.5 T MR, typically capturing 3–8 coronal slices. Postprocessing procedures involved registering each coronal slice image to a reference image in an intermediate respiratory position. Furthermore, automatic segmentation techniques were employed to delineate the lung parenchyma and eliminate pulmonary vessels with Otsu methods for variable thresholding. 10 Through the combination of automatically determined regions of interest along with heart frequencies, the complete cardiac cycle was reconstructed using a phase-sorting algorithm. For each slice, the perfusion weighting phase was automatically selected, and the perfusion value was normalised using the signal from the whole blood voxel defined in the middle slice. 13 Notably, the determination of the threshold plays a critical role in the calculation of QDP. In Pöhler et al ’s study, the threshold of PREFUL MRI for healthy perfusion values was defined as 1% of the full blood voxel signal value. 35 However, in the research conducted by Behrendt et al , 19 the threshold of PREFUL MRI was set at 2% and the threshold of DCE MRI was 1.75% for QDP analysis. Additionally, as taken in the study by Schiwek et al , 10 the calculation method involving variable thresholds rather than fixed thresholds is being increasingly adopted for both PREFUL MRI and DCE MRI. These differences in threshold determination across studies could potentially account for variations in the MD observed in our meta-analysis. Hyperpolarised gas MRI is a highly sensitive and specific imaging technique that directly visualises the distribution of ventilation within the lung. 36 On the other hand, PREFUL MRI is a method that uses regional lung motion during the breathing cycle to quantify regional ventilation (RV). It identifies ventilation defects, characterised by minimal signal changes or altered signal dynamics between inspiration and expiration. Although our meta-analysis demonstrates good agreement and strong correlation between PREFUL VDP and 129 Xe VDP, some variations persist, particularly in the study conducted by Couch et al . 28 These differences can be attributed, at least in part, to the influence of time-of-flight inflow effects, resulting in enhanced visibility of pulmonary vessels in single-slice, free-breathing 1 H images. The computation of VDP in PREFUL MRI primarily relies on two ventilation-derived maps: the RV map and the flow-volume loop (FVL) correlation map. The RV map quantifies the signal change between end inspiration and end expiration while correcting for volume errors resulting from image registration. 37 On the other hand, the FVL correlation map cross-correlates each voxel FVL in the lung parenchyma with a healthy reference FVL to generate a voxel FVL cross-correlation map, which is subsequently used to calculate the FVL-based VDP value. 38 Generally, for VDP RV , VDP is determined by identifying voxels with ventilation deficit, where all RV values below the 90th percentile multiplied by a factor of 0.4 are considered as such defects. Conversely, for VDP FVL , a fixed threshold of 0.9 is used to identify ventilation defects. 38 In our meta-analysis, the VDP values derived from PREFUL MRI were calculated based on VDP RV , which resulted in relatively consistent results among all included studies, with an MD of 0.34% (95% CI −4.94% to 5.62%) and a correlation coefficient of 0.73. The results indicate that the VDP measured by PREFUL and 129 Xe MRI was essentially consistent, with a difference of only 0.34% between the VDP values calculated by the two MRI imaging methods. This consistency in VDP outcomes may be attributed to the utilisation of VDP RV as the basis for VDP calculation across the studies. Previous studies have reported remarkable correlations between RV assessed by FD techniques and spirometry parameters, particularly FEV 1 . 35 39 Similarly, considerable correlations have been observed between PREFUL MRI-derived QDP and predicted FEV 1 for the whole lung. 13 19 20 However, on combining the correlation coefficients from the included studies, our results found that the correlation between QDP and FEV 1 (r=−0.51; 95% CI −0.74 to −0.18) was relatively weaker compared with that between VDP and FEV 1 (r=−0.60; 95% CI −0.73 to −0.44). This observation can be explained by the fact that QDP represents a perfusion parameter while FEV 1 reflects a ventilation parameter. Additionally, it should be noted that PREFUL MRI, unlike global lung function measurements such as FEV 1 , involves the calculation of QDP based on only 3–8 slices, resulting in incomplete coverage of the entire lung parenchyma. 19 The results from our meta-analysis hold significant implications for the future clinical application of PREFUL MRI, considering the crucial role of lung function assessment in the diagnosis and prognosis of pulmonary diseases. Moreover, the measurement of ventilation and perfusion is of remarkable importance in monitoring the efficacy of pharmacological interventions in hyperinflated patients with COPD and predicting adverse outcomes such as chronic lung allograft dysfunction-related mortality or transplant failure in large prospective cohorts of lung transplant recipients. 40 41 Finally, PREFUL MRI offers the advantage of simultaneously obtaining ventilation and perfusion parameters in a single examination, eliminating the need for breath-holding manoeuvres and contrast agent administration. This feature is particularly advantageous for patients with lung diseases who may have difficulties tolerating prolonged supine breath-holding examinations. Several limitations are associated with this meta-analysis. First, the sample size was comparatively modest, consisting of only 10 studies. Moreover, there was variation in the literature enrolled when examining different lung function indicators. Second, the diverse range of disease states encompassed in this study, including both healthy volunteers and patients with various conditions such as CF, introduces potential limitations in extrapolating the results to specific populations. Third, substantial heterogeneity was observed in the meta-analysis, but due to the limited number of available studies, subgroup analyses could not be conducted to explore potential sources of heterogeneity. Lastly, the quantification of lung function parameters using PREFUL MRI does not directly measure FEV 1 . Published studies have consistently shown a significant correlation between PREFUL lung function parameters and spirometry-based FEV 1 . Therefore, this study does not directly compare PREFUL MRI with spirometry-based FEV 1 . Conclusions PREFUL MRI is a promising innovative imaging for assessing lung function, as it exhibits satisfactory bias and LOA compared with DEC MRI and 129 Xe MRI. In the future, large-scale, multicentre, prospective studies will be needed to validate it. supplementary material online supplemental file 1 10.1136/bmjresp-2023-002198 online supplemental file 2 10.1136/bmjresp-2023-002198 Footnotes Funding: This work was supported by the Beijing Hospitals Authority Clinical Medicine Development of Special Funding Support (ZLRK202306), the Beijing Hospitals Authority’s Ascent Plan (DFL20220303) and the Beijing Key Specialists in Major Epidemic Prevention and Control. documents.title: Virtual reality in adults with respiratory diseases experiencing dyspnoea: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
documents.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Our aim was to evaluate virtual reality's effects in dyspnoea's management.
METHODS: Information sources: Trials were identified through a systematic search carried out on MEDLINE, Web of Science, Scopus and CINAHL until 17 March 2025.
ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA: Eligible studies were controlled trials including adults with dyspnoea associated with respiratory diseases, for whom virtual reality was implemented and compared with another intervention. Risk of bias: Risk of bias (ROB) was assessed using the ROB 2 tool.
SYNTHESIS OF RESULTS: The primary outcome was dyspnoea. Secondary outcomes included exercise capacity, health-related quality of life (HRQOL) and muscle function. Effect size was expressed using standardised mean difference (SMD) or MD for primary and secondary outcomes, respectively (random-effects model). We used the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation approach to judge the certainty of evidence.
RESULTS: Included studies: 13 studies were selected, including 483 adults and using non-immersive tools (n=7) or immersive tools (n=6). Risk of bias in these studies was low (n=1), some concerns (n=8) and high risk (n=4).
SYNTHESIS OF RESULTS: No difference was found in dyspnoea (8 studies, 224 participants; SMD 0.02, 95% CI -0.82 to 0.86, I2=88.2%), exercise capacity (5 studies, 183 participants; MD 3.62, 95% CI -19.39 to 26.63, I2=39.8%) and in HRQOL (4 studies, 127 participants; MD -11.81, 95% CI -42.95 to 19.33, I2=98.9%). The data available were insufficient to conduct a pooled analysis for muscle function.
CONCLUSIONS: Limitations of evidence: The evidence is very uncertain about virtual reality's effects on dyspnoea due to risk of bias, imprecision and heterogeneity.
INTERPRETATION: Further studies are needed and should explore various aspects of the application of immersive virtual reality.
PROSPERO REGISTRATION NUMBER: CRD42023443280.
documents.conclusions: Limitations of evidence: The evidence is very uncertain about virtual reality's effects on dyspnoea due to risk of bias, imprecision and heterogeneity.

See: http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/4.0/ . Abstract Objectives Our aim was to evaluate virtual reality’s effects in dyspnoea’s management. Methods Information sources: Trials were identified through a systematic search carried out on MEDLINE, Web of Science, Scopus and CINAHL until 17 March 2025. Eligibility criteria: Eligible studies were controlled trials including adults with dyspnoea associated with respiratory diseases, for whom virtual reality was implemented and compared with another intervention. Risk of bias: Risk of bias (ROB) was assessed using the ROB 2 tool. Synthesis of results: The primary outcome was dyspnoea. Secondary outcomes included exercise capacity, health-related quality of life (HRQOL) and muscle function. Effect size was expressed using standardised mean difference (SMD) or MD for primary and secondary outcomes, respectively (random-effects model). We used the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation approach to judge the certainty of evidence. Results Included studies: 13 studies were selected, including 483 adults and using non-immersive tools (n=7) or immersive tools (n=6). Risk of bias in these studies was low (n=1), some concerns (n=8) and high risk (n=4). Synthesis of results: No difference was found in dyspnoea (8 studies, 224 participants; SMD 0.02, 95% CI −0.82 to 0.86, I 2 =88.2%), exercise capacity (5 studies, 183 participants; MD 3.62, 95% CI −19.39 to 26.63, I 2 =39.8%) and in HRQOL (4 studies, 127 participants; MD −11.81, 95% CI −42.95 to 19.33, I 2 =98.9%). The data available were insufficient to conduct a pooled analysis for muscle function. Conclusions Limitations of evidence: The evidence is very uncertain about virtual reality’s effects on dyspnoea due to risk of bias, imprecision and heterogeneity. Interpretation: Further studies are needed and should explore various aspects of the application of immersive virtual reality. PROSPERO registration number CRD42023443280.
